concepts.name: Looking far away is looking back in time
concepts.why: Light from a distant galaxy has been on its way for as many years as the galaxy is light years away, so the farther we look, the older the universe we see. This is what lets cosmology compare the universe then with the universe now.
concepts.evidence: The book notes that the Andromeda galaxy is 2 million light years away, so the light now reaching us left it 2 million years ago, and that light from the most distant galaxy left it 14 billion years ago.

concepts.name: The cosmological red shift is the stretching of light by the expansion of space
concepts.why: Nearly every galaxy's hydrogen spectrum is shifted to the red by an amount proportional to its distance, and the explanation is that space itself is expanding. The reader should be able to say why this is not a Doppler shift and why every observer sees himself at rest with the others receding.
concepts.evidence: The book states that the photon wavelength is stretched in transit from the source to the observer, that doubling the distance doubles the red shift, and that there is no center of expansion in the universe.

concepts.name: Hubble's law, $\kv = H_{0}\kd$
concepts.why: The recession velocity of a galaxy is proportional to its distance, and the constant of proportionality is the Hubble constant. The law is the expansion of the universe put into one line.
concepts.evidence: The book gives $v = H_{0}d$ for galaxies farther away than about 50 Mly, with $H_{0}$ the slope of the velocity versus distance graph of Figure 34.5 and taken as 20 (km/s)/Mly.

concepts.name: Find a galaxy's recession speed from its distance, or its distance from its speed
concepts.why: With Hubble's law a measured red shift becomes a distance and a distance becomes a speed. The same arithmetic gives a rough age of the universe.
concepts.evidence: The book works a galaxy 100 Mly away, moving at 2000 km/s, and the section's problems ask how far away galaxies moving at 2.0% of the speed of light are (0.30 Gly) and how fast a galaxy 10 Gly away moves.

concepts.name: The cosmic microwave background is the cooled remnant of the Big Bang
concepts.why: If there was a Big Bang, its fireball should still fill space as blackbody radiation stretched to long wavelengths. Its discovery is the second great piece of evidence for an expanding universe.
concepts.evidence: The book tells how Gamow predicted the radiation and Penzias and Wilson detected it in 1964, and Figure 34.7(b) shows the most perfect blackbody spectrum known, at a temperature of 2.725 K.

concepts.name: A small asymmetry in the forces left the universe made of matter
concepts.why: The universe is nearly pure matter, although particle physics is almost symmetric between matter and antimatter. A tiny asymmetry in the early universe explains what survived the annihilation.
concepts.evidence: The book cites the absence of 0.511-MeV annihilation radiation from space and the decay of a neutral K-meson that favors matter, and explains that one part in $10^{9}$ more matter would leave the stars and galaxies we see.

concepts.name: The small wrinkles in the cosmic microwave background
concepts.why: Galaxies could not have formed without early fluctuations in density, so the background radiation cannot be perfectly smooth. It is extremely smooth, and that smoothness needs an explanation.
concepts.evidence: The book describes COBE's 1992 discovery of small fluctuations and WMAP's detailed map in Figure 34.8, temperature fluctuations of only 200 μK out of 2.7 K.

concepts.name: The epochs of the early universe follow the unification of the forces
concepts.why: Going back in time, the universe grows hotter and denser until the average particle energy reaches the energies at which the forces unify. The TOE, GUT and electroweak epochs are named for those unifications.
concepts.evidence: Figure 34.9 lays the evolution out on a logarithmic time scale, and the book places the electroweak epoch from $10^{-34}$ s to $10^{-11}$ s, the GUT epoch from $10^{-43}$ s to $10^{-34}$ s, and the TOE epoch before $10^{-43}$ s, at $10^{19}$ GeV.

concepts.name: Spontaneous symmetry breaking and the inflationary scenario
concepts.why: When the strong force separated from the electroweak force, the transition released energy that may have expanded the universe by a factor of $10^{50}$ or more in an instant. That inflation would stretch the early wrinkles nearly flat and so explain the smoothness of the background radiation.
concepts.evidence: The book describes Guth's proposal that the transition from GUT to electroweak, like a phase transition, drove expansion from $10^{-35}$ s to about $10^{-32}$ s, and notes that there is as yet no other plausible explanation for the smoothness of the CMBR.

concepts.name: Acceleration and gravity produce identical effects
concepts.why: A person in a closed elevator cannot tell whether it accelerates upward or stands in a gravitational field. Einstein took this to hold in all situations, and general relativity grows from it.
concepts.evidence: Figure 34.10 follows a beam of light across an accelerating elevator and a resting one, and the book concludes that, if acceleration affects light, gravity must too.

concepts.name: Gravity bends the path of light
concepts.why: Light has no mass, yet it falls in a gravitational field, because mass curves space and light follows the curve. The 1919 eclipse made this the first verification of general relativity.
concepts.evidence: Figure 34.11 shows starlight curved by the Sun so that the stars appear shifted from their known positions, and the book states that the bending was precisely what Einstein predicted.

concepts.name: Gravitational lensing
concepts.why: A galaxy between us and a more distant one bends its light like a converging lens and can form several images of it. Lensing is a large-scale test of general relativity and a check that red shift is proportional to distance.
concepts.evidence: Figure 34.12 shows light from a distant galaxy reaching the Earth along paths on both sides of an intermediary galaxy, and the book notes that each image has the same red shift, larger than that of the intermediary.

concepts.name: Black holes and the event horizon
concepts.why: An object whose escape velocity exceeds the speed of light lets nothing out. The event horizon is the distance at which the escape velocity is exactly the speed of light, and it is the edge of the black hole.
concepts.evidence: The book defines black holes as objects from which nothing, not even light, can escape, and describes the X rays of accretion disks (Figure 34.13) and the too-massive X-ray sources that make their existence widely accepted.

concepts.name: The Schwarzschild radius, $\kRS = 2GM/\kc^{2}$
concepts.why: The radius of the event horizon grows in proportion to the mass. Since $G$ is small and $c^{2}$ is large, a black hole of a few solar masses is only a few kilometers across.
concepts.evidence: The book gives $R_{\text{S}} = 2GM/c^{2}$ and states that the size of a black hole is twice $R_{\text{S}}$.

concepts.name: Find the Schwarzschild radius of a black hole of a given mass
concepts.why: The formula turns a mass into a size, from a stellar black hole to a supermassive one at a galaxy's core.
concepts.evidence: The section's problems find 23.6 km for eight solar masses and $2.95\times10^{12}\;\text{m}$, or $3.12\times10^{-4}$ ly, for $10^{9}$ Suns.

concepts.name: Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of supernovas
concepts.why: In a supernova the core's electrons and protons are forced together into neutrons, and the strong force halts the collapse at a star of nuclear density. A neutron star is slightly larger than a black hole of the same mass.
concepts.evidence: The book describes their discovery by Bell and Hewish in 1967 and states that a neutron star heavier than a certain limit must collapse to a black hole.

concepts.name: Gravitational waves
concepts.why: Moving masses should send ripples through space itself, as a water bug's foot sends waves across a pond. They travel at the speed of light and need extreme events to be detected.
concepts.evidence: The book cites the binary neutron star orbit measured by Taylor and Hulse and the first direct detection by LIGO in 2015, shown in Figure 34.15.

concepts.name: Quantum gravity and the radiation of black holes
concepts.why: Where gravity is strong enough to act on the quantum scale, quantum mechanics and general relativity must be used together. A black hole can then radiate, as pairs created near its horizon split and one member escapes.
concepts.evidence: Figure 34.17 shows particle-antiparticle pairs created just outside the event horizon, and the book states that black holes shrink by this process, extremely slowly, on the order of $10^{67}$ years for a solar-mass hole.

concepts.name: Superstring theory treats fundamental particles as vibrating strings
concepts.why: Superstring theory is an attempt at a Theory of Everything, and so must contain quantum gravity. Its particles, the graviton among them, act like one-dimensional vibrating strings in a superspace whose extra dimensions curled up as the forces separated.
concepts.evidence: The book states the main tenet of the theory and ties the curling up of dimensions to spontaneous symmetry breaking after the Big Bang.

concepts.name: There may be a smallest length and a shortest time
concepts.why: Quantum gravity suggests that space and time are grainy, with no meaning to intervals shorter than some tiny finite size. Superstrings would sit at that limit, with no further substructure.
concepts.evidence: The book places the smallest size at about $10^{-35}$ m and the shortest time between $10^{-43}$ s and $10^{-95}$ s, and the section's problem compares the energy of a photon of wavelength $10^{-35}$ m with the $10^{19}$ GeV of unification.

concepts.name: Galaxies rotate with a nearly flat velocity curve
concepts.why: If a galaxy's mass were concentrated at its center, like its luminous stars, the orbital speed of its stars would fall off with distance. The measured speed stays almost constant, and that is the first evidence for dark matter.
concepts.evidence: Figure 34.18 shows Doppler-shifted light from the two sides of a rotating galaxy and a graph of velocity versus distance that stays near 200 to 250 km/s far beyond the bright center.

concepts.name: Dark matter
concepts.why: There is about ten times as much mass in the universe as in the luminous objects we see, and we do not know what it is. Its amount bears on whether the universe expands forever.
concepts.evidence: The book describes the work of Zwicky and Rubin, the mass of galactic clusters and their halos, and the X rays of hot gas between galaxies in Figure 34.18(c).

concepts.name: The critical density, $\krhoc \approx 10^{-26}\;\text{kg/m}^{3}$
concepts.why: The critical density is the average density that would just halt universal expansion in a universe with no cosmological constant. It amounts to a few nucleons per cubic meter.
concepts.evidence: The book gives $\rho_{\text{c}} \approx 10^{-26}\;\text{kg/m}^{3}$, good to about a factor of two, and states that luminous matter accounts for roughly 0.5% to 2% of it.

concepts.name: Open, closed and flat universes
concepts.why: An open universe is negatively curved and expands forever, a closed one is positively curved and returns a traveler to the start, and a flat one lies between. Measurements with the cosmological constant show the universe is very close to flat.
concepts.evidence: The book explains closure as a question of gravitation and the cosmological constant, and states that the universe is expanding faster now than in the past.

concepts.name: MACHOs and microlensing
concepts.why: Small dark bodies in a galaxy's halo would not block a star's light but would focus it, and the star would brighten in a characteristic manner. Such searches test whether dark matter is ordinary matter.
concepts.evidence: The book states that a few MACHOs have been observed, but not predominantly in galactic halos nor in the numbers needed, and the section's problem counts how many MACHOs dark matter would require.

concepts.name: Neutrino oscillations and neutrino mass
concepts.why: A neutrino can change flavor only if it has mass, since a massless neutrino travels at the speed of light and no time passes for it. Oscillations would explain the missing solar neutrinos and could supply some of the dark matter.
concepts.evidence: The book reports convincing evidence of oscillations from the Super-Kamiokande detector from 1999 on, and the low count of electron neutrinos from the Sun.

concepts.name: WIMPs, previously unknown particles as dark matter
concepts.why: The most radical proposal is that dark matter is chargeless, weakly interacting massive particles of a completely new kind. They would gather in halos rather than coalesce into spirals.
concepts.evidence: The book names neutralinos and axions as proposed WIMPs and states that all explanations from known matter must be shown inferior before WIMPs are accepted.

concepts.name: Complexity, the study of complex adaptive systems
concepts.why: Complex systems obey the simple laws of physics yet may reveal patterns simple systems do not, above all the ability to adapt, organize themselves and evolve.
concepts.evidence: The book's examples include the primordial ocean and the emergence of life, economic systems, cultures, science and language, and crystal growth and magnetic domains in physics.

concepts.name: Chaos is extreme sensitivity to initial conditions
concepts.why: A chaotic system's outcome changes tremendously with a small change in where it starts, so its long-term behavior cannot be predicted with precision. Chaotic systems may be simple, like a double pendulum, or complex.
concepts.evidence: The book's examples are the orbit of Pluto, a decaying satellite, a chaotic heartbeat, and vortices in a fluid.

concepts.name: Chaos can hold order and self-organization
concepts.why: There can be organization in chaos, and it can be quantified. Some chaotic systems settle into a stable self-organized form.
concepts.evidence: Figure 34.21 shows the infinitely fine patterns of the Mandelbrot set, and Figure 34.22 the Great Red Spot, stable for at least 400 years amid Jupiter's chaotic vortices.

concepts.name: High-temperature superconductors
concepts.why: A superconductor has zero resistivity below its critical temperature. Ceramics found since 1986 superconduct above 77 K, the boiling point of cheap liquid nitrogen, which is what makes them economically interesting.
concepts.evidence: Figure 34.23 shows mercury's resistivity dropping to zero at 4.2 K, and the book traces critical temperatures from 35 K in 1986 to 125 K by 1988.

concepts.name: A superconductor excludes magnetic flux
concepts.why: A superconductor keeps magnetic flux out and so repels a magnet. A magnet floating above a cooled sample is the evidence that it is superconducting.
concepts.evidence: Figure 34.24 shows a magnet levitated above a high-temperature superconductor cooled by liquid nitrogen, which comes to rest on the sample when it warms.

concepts.name: Compare the cost of cooling a superconductor with the energy a normal wire wastes
concepts.why: A superconducting wire pays only when its coolant costs less than the energy a normal wire loses to heat. The comparison uses the power dissipated in a resistance and the price of electric energy.
concepts.evidence: The section's problem finds that a normal wire of 0.30 Ω carrying 100 A wastes as much as one liter of liquid nitrogen per hour costs.

concepts.name: Forefront results must be reproducible
concepts.why: A result at the frontier is accepted only when it can be reproduced or is of such quality that a single observation is meaningful. Reports of superconductors above 200 K have not passed that test.
concepts.evidence: Figure 34.25(a) shows one sample tried three times, superconducting near 230 K once and not at all in the other trials, and the book calls such samples unidentified superconducting objects.

concepts.name: Open questions on the largest, intermediate and smallest scales
concepts.why: Part of discovery is knowing which questions to ask, and the book gathers the questions physicists now know to ask on three scales. Each rests on the physics the reader has already met.
concepts.evidence: The book asks, among others, whether the universe is open or closed and what dark matter is, how phase transitions happen molecule by molecule and how high-$T_{\text{c}}$ superconductors work, and why there are three families of quarks and leptons and whether the proton is stable.

concepts.name: The largest and smallest scales answer each other
concepts.why: Many of the open questions of cosmology have answers in particle physics, and the reverse. The closure of the universe, for example, depends on the type and number of particles that may contribute to it.
concepts.evidence: The book ties the question of an open or closed universe to small-scale physics, and whether neutrinos have mass to both the closure of the universe and the patterns of particle physics.
